passages.original: Quam magnos studiosis afferat fructus scientia dividend i ,qua'IJque apud peripateticamdisciplinam, semper hæc fuerit in honore notitia,docet et Andronici, diligentissimi senis, de divisione liber editus, et hic idem a Plotino gravissimo philosopho com- probatus,et in libri Platonis,qui Sophistes inscribitur,commentariis a Porphyrio repetitus, et ab eodem per hanc,introduclionis laudata in Categorias utilitas.Dicit enim fore necessarium generis,speciei differentiae proprii, accidentisque peritiam, cum propter alia multajtum propter utilitatem quae est maxima partiendi.Quare quoniam maximus usus est facillimaque doctrina,ego quoque id,sicutpleraque omnia, Romar.is auribus tradens,introductionismodo,habitaque in eamdemrem,et competentisubtilique tractatione,et moderata brevitate,perscripsi,ut nec anxietas decisas orationis, et non perfectse sententiæ,legentium mentibus ingeratur;nec putetsupervacuam loquacitatem harum reruminexperiens, rudis, insolensque novi, audientium mentes habere ;
passages.english: How great are the benefits that the science of dividing brings to students, and how this knowledge has always been held in honour in the Peripatetic school, is shown by the book On Division published by Andronicus, a most diligent old man; by this same [book] having been approved by Plotinus, a most weighty philosopher; by its being taken up again by Porphyry in his commentaries on the book of Plato entitled the Sophist; and by the usefulness of the Introduction to the Categories, praised by the same [Porphyry] on account of it. For he says that skill in genus, species, difference, property and accident is necessary, both for many other reasons and on account of the usefulness of dividing, which is very great. Therefore, since its use is very great and its teaching very easy, I too, handing this on to Roman ears as I have nearly everything else, have written it out in the manner of an introduction, with a treatment of the subject that is both fitting and precise, and with moderate brevity, so that neither the anxiety of a cut-off discourse and an incomplete thought may be forced upon the minds of readers, nor may someone inexperienced in these matters, untrained and unused to what is new, suppose that the minds of the listeners are burdened with superfluous wordiness;
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'dividend i' for 'dividendi', 'qua'IJque' for 'quamque', 'introduclionis'). The final clause ('nec putet ... mentes habere') is syntactically awkward; rendered as 'suppose that the minds of the listeners [are given/have] superfluous wordiness'; the sense is approximate.

passages.original: Sunt autem oppositiones quatuor, aut ut contraria, ut bonum malo ;aut ut habituset privatio,ut visus et cæcitas.Quanquarn sintetquaedam res in quibus discernere difficultas sit utrum in contrariis an in privationeet habitu easoporteat collocari, ut sant motus, quies, sanitas, aegritudo, vigilatio,somnus, lux,tenebrae. Sed haec alias, nunc de reliquis oppositionibusdicendum est.Tertia oppositio est quae est secundum affirmationcm et ne- gationem, ut Socrates vivit, Socrates non vivit. Quarta secundum relationem,ut pater,filius,dominus,servus.Secundum quas igitur harum oppositionum quatuor divisio generis sit,rectissima ratione monstrandumest.Manifestumestenimet oppositiones esse quatuor,et genera etspecies per opposita separari.Nunc ergo dicendum est secundum quam oppositionem harum quatuor vel quemadmodum speciesa generedisjungi conveniat,et prima quidem sit contradictionis oppositio.Voco autem contradictionis oppositionem quae affirmatione et negatione proponi tur.
passages.english: Now there are four [kinds of] opposition: either as contraries, as good to evil; or as possession and privation, as sight and blindness. Although there are also certain things in which it is difficult to discern whether they ought to be placed among contraries or among privation and possession, such as motion and rest, health and sickness, waking and sleep, light and darkness. But [more on] these elsewhere; now we must speak of the remaining oppositions. The third opposition is that which is according to affirmation and negation, as 'Socrates is alive', 'Socrates is not alive'. The fourth is according to relation, as father and son, master and slave. We must therefore show by the most correct reasoning according to which of these four oppositions the division of a genus takes place. For it is clear both that there are four oppositions and that genera and species are separated by opposites. Now, then, we must say according to which of these four oppositions, or in what way, it is fitting for species to be separated from the genus; and let the first be the opposition of contradiction. I call the opposition of contradiction that which is set out by affirmation and negation.

passages.original: Aristoteles enim haec in Topicis diligenter praecepit, ut in his quae dicuntur bona, alia sunt bona,ut ea quae boni retinent qualitatem, alia quae ipsa quidem nulla qualitate dicuntur,sed quod bonam rem faciunt, idcirco bona dicuntur. Oportet autem maxime exercere hanc arlem,ut ipse Aristoteles ait,contra sophisticas importunitates.Si enim nulla subjecta sit res quam significat vox,designalivaesse non dicitur ; sin vero una res sit quam significat vox,dicitursimplex; quod si plures,multiplex,id est multa significans.
passages.english: For Aristotle carefully laid this down in the Topics: among the things that are called good, some are good in that they possess the quality of the good, while others are called [good] not by any quality of their own, but are called good for this reason, that they produce a good thing. And, as Aristotle himself says, one must above all practise this art against the annoyances of the sophists. For if there is no underlying thing that a word signifies, it is said not to be significant; but if there is one thing that the word signifies, it is called simple; and if several, multiple, that is, signifying many things.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected: 'arlem' read as 'artem' (art); 'designalivaesse' read as 'designativa esse' (significant). The syntax of the first sentence is loose in the Latin ('ut ... alia sunt bona ... alia quae ... dicuntur'), and it has been rendered by sense.
